title: Scalable fabrication of high activity nanoporous copper powders for electrochemical CO2 reduction via ball milling and dealloying
abstract: Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) is a promising technology to close the anthropic CO2 circle using renewable energy to achieve carbon neutrality. Future commercialization of ECR will require the development of new catalyst synthesis routes that will allow significant upscaling of catalyst production from current research-level milligram quantities to the kilogram scale and beyond while maintaining the activity and selectivity demonstrated at the research level. In this work, we report on generating and testing submicron-sized nanoporous copper (npCu) particles by using a scalable approach consisting of ball milling brittle Cu-based intermetallics followed by dealloying to add nanoporosity for high surface area. The resulting npCu particles have been tested in an industry-relevant large area (25 cm2) electrolyzer platform and showed Faraday efficiencies (FE) for ethylene up to 34 % at current densities of 75− 100 mA/cm2 while keeping FE for hydrogen less than 30 %. Our results demonstrate that a combination of ball milling and dealloying is a promising approach to generate large quantities of high activity and high surface area npCu particles for ECR at an industry-relevant scale.

Electrochemical CO2reduction Scale-Up Dealloying Copper Ethylene production
A B S T R A C T
Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) is a promising technology to close the anthropic CO2 circle using renewable energy to achieve carbon neutrality. Future commercialization of ECR will require the development of new catalyst synthesis routes that will allow significant upscaling of catalyst production from current research-level milligram quantities to the kilogram scale and beyond while maintaining the activity and selectivity demonstrated at the research level. In this work, we report on generating and testing submicron-sized nanoporous copper (npCu) particles by using a scalable approach consisting of ball milling brittle Cu-based intermetallics followed by dealloying to add nanoporosity for high surface area. The resulting npCu particles have been tested in an industry-relevant large area (25 cm2) electrolyzer platform and showed Faraday efficiencies (FE) for ethylene up to 34 % at current densities of 75− 100 mA/cm2 while keeping FE for hydrogen less than 30 %. Our results demonstrate that a combination of ball milling and dealloying is a promising approach to generate large quantities of high activity and high surface area npCu particles for ECR at an industry-relevant scale.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Electrochemical CO2 reduction (ECR) enables the conversion of the greenhouse gas CO2 into value-added chemical products [1–7] thus providing a pathway towards a carbon-neutral economy if powered by renewable electrical energy. With rapidly decreasing prices for renewable electric energy, ECR becomes increasingly cost competitive [8]. Much research has been devoted to further increase ECR catalyst activity and selectivity. ECR catalysts range from metals (Cu, Ag, Au, Bi, Sn, and etc.) to carbons, metal-organic-framework, and etc [6,9–17]. Most basic and applied research in this field focuses on Cu which is unique in that it efficiently converts CO2 to C2 and C3 products that can be used as fuels or feedstock for the chemical industry; other catalysts predominately or exclusively generate C1 products [18].
To impact global CO2 emissions, a dramatic scale-up of the ECR technology will be necessary. This requires not only the development of a scalable electrolyzer technology like that used in the water electrolysis industry [19], but also upscaling synthesis and integration of inexpensive, stable, active, and selective Cu-based catalysts. However, traditional catalyst research is performed at the milligram scale, and while
these experimental catalysts may show excellent performance, scale-up of fabrication and integration may be difficult to achieve. Thus, the development of scalable ECR catalyst preparation procedures is a critical area that needs to be addressed.
Ball milling has been widely employed in various industries to produce metal powders at the metric tons scale [20]. It is not only an economically-viable route towards metal powders but also provides a path to non-equilibrium alloy compositions and intermetallics that otherwise are difficult to realize [21,22]. Combined with dealloying, it becomes a powerful method for fabricating large quantities of nanoporous high surface area metal powders. Dealloying is a corrosion process where one or more of the less noble elements of an alloy are selectively etched away, leaving behind a characteristic high surface area pore-ligament nanomorphology [23–29]. While ball milling processes are typically used to create relatively large, micron-sized particles, dealloying provides a straightforward route for integration of nanoporosity. The resulting nanoporous particle morphology is expected to facilitate the formation of gas/solid/electrolyte triple phase boundaries that are required for high performance, high current density gas-diffusion electrolyzer electrodes. In this study, we demonstrate a

scalable production pathway for nanoporous copper (npCu) powders using a combination of ball milling and dealloying. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that attempts to address the catalyst production capacity needs of the emerging ECR industry. Our npCu particle fabrication process is highly efficient with a yield of almost 100 % with respect to the Cu content of the Al2Cu starting alloy, or 50 % by weight where the missing 50 wt% can be attributed to leached aluminum that can be recycled if desired. The resulting npCu powder was integrated in an industrially-relevant gas diffusion electrolyzer design and showed high activity towards ECR: The total Faradaic efficiencies (FE) towards ECR and the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) reached 81 % at 150 mA/cm2. The ECR specific FE for the detected ECR products CO, CH4, and C2H4 peaked at 34 % for current densities of 75 and 100 mA/cm2 which is within the cost/profit margin considerations for commercial ECR applications.

sections.heading: 2. Materials and Methods
sections.text:
A θ-phase Al2Cu ingot (50 g) was prepared by melting pure Al (99.999 %, Alfa Aesar) and Cu (99.999 %, Alfa Aesar) metal powders in a graphite crucible in an induction furnace (MTI, SP-15TC). The crucible filled with the metal powders was heated to 750 ◦C and kept at that temperature for 10 min before cooling down naturally in the furnace. The resulting Al2Cu ingot was pre-crushed (Retsch BB50 Jaw Crusher) to particles smaller than 2 mm. The ball milling process (2000 rpm for 8 h) was performed using a Retsch Emax ball mill. 12 mL of the pre-crushed Al2Cu powder and 30 mL 2 mm zirconia grinding balls were mixed in a 50 mL zirconia grinding jar. For ECR testing, we dealloyed 2 g of the resulting Al2Cu powder in 50 mL of 6 M KOH solution until hydrogen evolution was no longer observed. To avoid violent reaction and splattering the powder was added slowly to the KOH solution. The resulting npCu powder was rinsed several times with DI water and dried in a vacuum desiccator before further characterization and testing. Particle size analysis of the as-prepared Al2Cu powder was performed using a laser scattering particle size distribution analyzer (HORIBA LA-960). Microstructural characterization of both as-milled and dealloyed samples was carried out using scanning electron microscopy (SEM, JEOL 7410) with lower secondary electron detector at an accelerating voltage of 5− 10 keV and a working distance of 8 mm.
For spray coating the gas diffusion layer (GDL), 1 g of the npCu catalyst powder was ultrasonically suspended in 20 mL isopropyl alcohol (Fig. 1a). Four 25 cm2 GDLs (Sigracet, 39BCE) were fixed on a substrate using scotch tape and coated with the npCu/isopropyl alcohol suspension using a handheld airbrush (Fig. 1b and c). The manual airbrush technique used in this work resulted in non-uniform catalysts coatings as indicted by color variations of the coated GDL. The npCuGDL cathode assemblies were integrated into a 25 cm2 Opus 12 Inc. gas diffusion electrolyzer using an Aemion™ AF1-HNN8− 50-X alkaline exchange membrane (AEM) (Ionomr Innovations Inc.) to separate the npCu-coated GDL cathode from the IrOx-coated porous Ti anode. The cell configuration is similar to that described in our previous work on CO2 to CO reduction using a nanoporous Au catalyst [30], and a
schematic representation of the setup can be found in Fig. 1d. The cathode-AEM-anode assembly was then compressed between two flow fields against the respective cell current collectors. A CO2 flow rate of 250 sccm was used on the cathode side of the cell while 0.5 M KOH was circulated via a peristaltic pump on the anode side at 60 mL/min. Electrolysis was run in constant current mode with 35-minute holds at 25, 50, 75, 100, and 150 mA/cm2. The as-generated gas products were measured with an in-line gas chromatograph (GC, SRI 8610C) equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) and a thermal conductivity detector (TCD) for measuring CO, CH4, C2H4, and H2 yields, respectively. The GC sampled the gas phase products every seven minutes and five data points were recorded for each current density. Here, we report the averaged selectivity and partial current densities (with the corresponding error bars) of the above GC-detected gas products. Liquid products are not reported here as the electrolyzer design used in this work did not allow for catholyte collection.

sections.heading: 3. Results
sections.text:
After milling for 8 h, the two-plus millimeter Al2Cu alloy particles were broken down into fine powders. SEM characterization reveals that most of the particles are smaller than 10 μm, though some particles as big as 20 μm can be found (Fig. 2a). Higher magnification SEM micrographs show the irregular shape and rough surface of the Al2Cu alloy particles. Some particles are smaller than 1 μm (Fig. 2b) suggesting the potential of using this approach to prepare powders with particles sizes considerably below one micron that can be used for preparing stable suspensions for spray coating. Indeed, high-energy ball milling can generate powders with an average particle size considerably below 100 nm [31]. Laser scattering particle size distribution analysis shows that the size distribution of the as-milled powder peaks at 7 μm with most of the particles being between 2 and 20 μm (Fig. 2c) in good agreement with the SEM observations. Ball milling at 2000 rpm and starting with Al2Cu particles allowed us to use much shorter milling times compared to previous work using lower rotation speeds and starting with pure Al and Cu powders [32]. Starting with pre-alloyed particles has two benefits: first, the alloy does not need to be formed during ball billing thus allowing for shorter ball billing times and providing better compositional uniformity; and second, the intermetallic phase Al2Cu is brittle which allows for fast breakdown of the particles during the ball milling process by preventing cold welding known from ball milling ductile metals in absence of a solvent.
High surface area npCu particles were obtained by selectively leaching the Al from the ball milled Al2Cu particles in 6 M KOH. Dealloying is a simple approach to prepare nanomaterials with precision control over the microstructures. Typically, dealloying is used to generate centimeter-sized monolithic nanoporous metals with uniform pore/ligament size [26]. The size of the ligaments (and the pores) can be adjusted by controlling the surface diffusion of the remaining more noble alloy component, for example, by the nature and concentration of the etch solution, dealloying time, and post-treatment such as annealing [33]. Here, we used dealloying to generate npCu particles with
Z. Qi et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 45 (2021) 101454
well-defined particle and pore/ligament size distributions. While we used only one gram of the Al2Cu starting alloy, the approach can be easily scaled up as both ball milling and dealloying are scalable processes: Commercial ball mills can produce powders at tons scale and Raney Nickel production (produced by dealloying Ni-Al alloys) is approaching 30,000 tons/year [34]. The shape of the nanoporous Cu particles (Fig. 3a) remains similar to that of the as-milled powders (Fig. 2b), but higher resolution SEM micrographs reveal the presence of a bicontinuous nanoscale ligament-pore morphology with ~30 nm ligaments and pores characteristic for dealloyed metals (Fig. 3b). Dealloying an alloy powder instead of a monolithic bulk sample reduces the dealloying time significantly, from days to hours. The shorter dealloying time required for powders limits coarsening of the nanoscale ligament-pore structure that is typically observed during prolonged exposure to the dealloying solution [35]. Therefore, the powder approach also enables the generation of smaller feature size (ligaments and pores) nanoporous metal particles. A simple geometrical calculation
shows that for our 7-micron average diameter npCu particle the integrated nanoporosity increases the electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) by a factor of about 30 (npCu with relative density of 0.3 and a gravimetric surface area of 10 m2/g for 30 nm diameter ligaments). It is likely that the nanopores will be filled with liquid electrolyte due spontaneous, capillary-force driven imbibition [36] thus providing the backbone for a stable three-dimensional triple phase interface that is essential for gas diffusion electrode (GDE) applications that require effective transport of electrons, protons, and CO2. The micron-scale pores formed by the npCu particle packing further facilitate the transport of both CO2 and ECR products in and out of the gas diffusion electrode.
The ECR performance of 25 cm2 npCu/GDL assemblies (Fig. 1c) was evaluated using an industrially-relevant 25 cm2 gas diffusion CO2 electrolyzer. This electrolyzer technology is scalable, thus providing a path forward towards large scale deployments of ECR. The npCu powders were integrated by spray coating the gas diffusion layer using a handheld air-brush. CO2 gas was directly fed into the electrolyzer and the products were analyzed using an inline GC. It should be noted that the electrolyzer design used in this work is optimized for efficiency and does not allow the use of a reference electrode to measure the cathode potential. Therefore, only current densities and device voltages are reported here. For each current density, five measurements were performed and the corresponding average values with error bars are shown in Fig. 4a. We observed steady-state operation of the electrolyzer over the entire measurement as demonstrated by the small error bars for each of the detected species over the entire current density range from 50 mA/cm2 to 150 mA/cm2. The total FE for gas phase products increases with increasing current density, from 58 % at 50 mA/cm2 to 81 % at 150 mA/cm2 (Fig. 4a). From our experience with microfluidic flow
Z. Qi et al.
Journal of CO2 Utilization 45 (2021) 101454
cell reactors, we expect that the missing FE can be attributed to liquid ECR products including formate, acetate, ethanol and propanol. Over the same current density range, FE for C2H4 shows a maximum of 34 % at 75 mA/cm2 with lower FEs for both lower (30 % @ 50 mA/cm2) and higher current densities (19 % @ 150 mA/cm2). The FE for CH4 and H2 increase with increasing current density, from 1% to 10 % and 23%– 48%, respectively, while FE for CO decreases from 8% to 3%. The increase in the partial current density of C2H4, j(C2H4), slows down with increasing current density while the increase in j(H2) accelerates with increasing current density (Fig. 4b). j(CH4) scales approximately linear with the current density while j(CO) remains relatively constant. FE and partial current densities for hydrocarbon products are significantly higher compared to Cu electrodes tested in H-cell configurations [1,2,4, 32].
Despite the inhomogeneous nature of the catalyst coating suggested by optical inspection, the performance of different GDE’s was very similar. For example, at a current density of 100 mA/cm2, the sample-tosample variation of both the total faradaic efficiency for ECR gas phase products (CO, CH4, and C2H4) and for the total FE (HER + ECR) was only 3%. We conclude that the results reflect the average response of the catalyst coating. In general, the ECR performance of catalysts in a gasdiffusion electrolyzer environment strongly depends on the way the catalyst is integrated [30,37]. Thus, while the ECR performance of our npCu catalyst coatings is already promising in terms of product yield and current density, we believe that improving integration (more uniform
coatings, optimized coating thickness) holds potential for further improving the ECR performance of our npCu catalyst.
We also want to point out that our npCu particles are stable in high pH environments. Using KOH for the dealloying process has the advantage that the npCu particles already have assumed a morphology that is stable in high pH environments thus allowing to use our npCu particle catalyst in flow cell electrolyzer designs that include a high pH catholyte junction. The cost of dealloying can be further reduced by using galvanic dealloying methods [38] that require no consumables and facilitate recycling of the dissolved metals for making new alloys. The ball milling technique can generate significantly smaller CuAl precursor alloy particles than the micrometer-sized particles used in the current work, and the effect of using finer npCu powders as well as further integration optimization on the ECR performance will the subject of future work.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusion
sections.text:
Nanoporous copper powders were fabricated from an Al2Cu starting alloy using a combination of ball milling and dealloying. The resulting nanoporous copper powders were integrated onto a 25 cm2 gas diffusion electrolyzer for electrochemical CO2 reduction and tested at high current densities ranging from 50 to 150 mA/cm2. FE for ethylene of up to 34 % was achieved at 75 mA/cm2. The nanoporous nature of these powders is ideal for applications that require high surface area such as catalytic and electrocatalytic applications. Our approach holds the promise of producing nanoporous metal powders at large scales relevant to addressing the needs for industrially-relevant ECR applications.
